findings.problem: CLIENT-F2 places the `messages` INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE revoke and the BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE guard trigger in messaging Stage 1 ("add the BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger and the revoke to Stage 1"). Stage 1 is server-only and the entire installed fleet sends chat by direct PostgREST insert — verified at E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/chat_repository.dart:228, :249, :279, :309. messaging.md Stage 1 states the opposite requirement explicitly: "Add the BEFORE INSERT trigger that assigns cseq under the same lock for any insert not arriving through the RPC, so the old fleet's direct PostgREST inserts stay contiguous during rollout." The first build that calls send_message is Stage 2, and messaging Stage 2 itself falls back to the direct insert. This is a sideloaded app behind a disguised launcher with no update channel (client.md §L: "a bad stage cannot be pulled back"), so revoking INSERT at Stage 1 makes every message send fail with a permission error for every user until they manually sideload a new APK.
findings.repair: Move the INSERT revoke to messaging Stage 10 (cleanup), gated on observed fleet composition via app_runtime_config.min_client_build — the same gate Stage 10 already applies to dropping messages.seq. The BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE guard trigger may land at Stage 1 (verified: the client issues no direct UPDATE or DELETE on messages; chat_repository.dart:185 and :206 are SELECTs), but the INSERT revoke may not. Until the revoke lands, the enforcement of the mutation rule is the four SECURITY DEFINER RPCs plus the guard trigger plus the canary, and CLIENT-F2 must say so rather than assuming D4-level privileges exist at Stage 1.

findings.problem: R1's invariant_after (d) defines the permanent canary as "contiguity of messages.cseq per couple and of couple_stream.pos per couple" — i.e. ROW contiguity. messaging.md's named invariant is the exact opposite: "ISSUED-RANGE CONTIGUITY, NOT ROW CONTIGUITY ... Contiguity is a property of the ISSUED cseq range (chat_streams.last_seq), never of the rows physically present." Deleting that distinction re-installs, server-side, the assertion messaging.md deleted as the cause of FATAL 2. It is reachable in production on the second clear: clear_conversation_everyone allocates a cseq for the clear control row and hard-deletes rows at or below it (verified, clear_chat_everyone.sql / chat_media_cleanup.sql do a bare `delete from public.messages where couple_id = v_couple_id`), and both messaging.md open decision 4 and CLIENT-F2 state "the clear row itself is never deleted by a subsequent clear." After clear#1 at cseq K1 and clear#2 at K2, the surviving rows are {K1} ∪ {K2} ∪ (K2, head] — a hole between K1 and K2. The canary goes red and stays red, on the one check R1 itself calls "the only place the load-bearing invariant is observable in production," which is precisely the muted-alarm failure data.md names as its own ceiling.
findings.repair: Define the canary as four predicates, none of them row contiguity: (i) couple_cursor.chat_seq >= max(messages.cseq) per couple; (ii) unique(couple_id, cseq) holds and cseq is NOT NULL; (iii) contiguity of rows only over cseq > coalesce(max(clear_through_cseq), 0); (iv) every surviving row at or below that floor has kind='clear'. Apply the same shape to couple_stream.pos, measured over (compaction floor, head], since couple_stream_compact deletes a prefix at pos <= min(applied_pos).

findings.problem: R1 specifies chat allocation as a single statement: "A chat stream-mutating operation executes: UPDATE couple_cursor SET chat_seq = chat_seq + 1 WHERE couple_id = ? RETURNING chat_seq" and "incremented in ONE UPDATE under ONE row lock held to COMMIT." For send_message that increments before the dedup check, which inverts messaging.md's stated ordering: "upsert the chat_streams row (no-op in the normal case), then lock it FOR UPDATE — the lock comes first, before anything else; look up (couple_id, sender_id, client_msg_id); if found, return the original ... without bumping the counter," and its rationale "Because the lock precedes the dedup check, a concurrent duplicate cannot burn a counter value. Holes in the issued range are impossible, not unlikely." Retry is the normal case in this design ("No network error is ever terminal. Retry is forever"), so every retry of a send the server already committed would consume a cseq that names no row. Under F2's canary that is a permanent hole; under any reading it deletes a property messaging.md declares server-enforced.
findings.repair: State chat allocation as two statements under one lock: SELECT couple_id FROM couple_cursor WHERE couple_id = ? FOR UPDATE, then the dedup lookup, then UPDATE couple_cursor SET chat_seq = chat_seq + 1 RETURNING chat_seq only on the non-duplicate path. Non-chat streams keep the single UPDATE because they have no dedup branch. The phrase "one UPDATE" is the part that breaks it and must be removed.

findings.problem: R1 asserts "Restoring density costs one extra bigint column on a row that is already locked. Nothing is paid for it." That is false. Postgres row locks are per-tuple, not per-column, so putting chat_seq and next_pos on one couple_cursor row makes every chat write serialize against every reach, capsule, closer and call-signal write for that couple. messaging.md's separate chat_streams row did not have that coupling. The concrete cost lands on calling: clear_conversation_everyone holds the allocator row lock for the whole transaction, and that transaction also deletes storage.objects rows joined against messages and then deletes every message row across 32 hash partitions (verified in chat_media_cleanup.sql). Under R1, call signalling allocates from next_pos on the same tuple (R1: "§I is unaffected — call signalling still uses stream='call' on couple_stream"), so a partner tapping Clear chat blocks the answer/ICE appends of a call in flight, inside calling.md's 45 s ring window, which calling.md already records as "routinely does not fit." transport.md accepted this blocking only for its own bulk purge ("briefly blocking the partner's sends"); it never accepted it across domains.
findings.repair: Keep one allocator TABLE and two ROWS: couple_cursor(couple_id, counter_kind) primary key, counter_kind in ('chat','stream'). The deadlock argument survives unchanged (no function body takes both), R1's CI assertion "no second allocator table exists" survives verbatim, and the two lock domains stay independent. If one row is kept, add the missing rule: no transaction may hold the allocator lock across a bulk DELETE — clear allocates the cseq, inserts the control row and commits; the delete runs in a second, batched transaction, which is safe because the control row carrying clear_through_cseq is the authoritative signal and a crash between the two is a retryable no-op.

findings.problem: R1 withdraws transport's (created_at, id) backfill ordering for every table and mandates "(id) unless it has a server-assigned monotone column." Verified on disk: every streamed entity table uses `id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid()` — schema.sql:44, :57, :65, :74, :85; reach_events.sql:9; capsules.sql:18, :30; intimacy_tables.sql:40, :61, :73, :97, :111. gen_random_uuid() is UUIDv4, so ordering by id is ordering at random. The rule therefore assigns historical stream_pos in arbitrary order and every client renders the entire pre-migration history of reaches, capsules, closer content and the rest shuffled. The defect the rule exists to prevent (a client-set created_at) misorders only the rows a client forged; the rule itself misorders all of them. R1 presents this as the strictly safer choice.
findings.repair: Backfill non-chat streamed tables by (created_at, id), as transport.md had it, and state the residual explicitly: a row whose created_at a client forged sorts wrongly once, in history only, and cannot create a gap because contiguity is over the issued range. messages keeps (seq, id) because seq is server-assigned. If a table is later found to have had a genuinely adversarial created_at, that table is backfilled by (created_at, id) with a documented manual correction, not by (id).

findings.problem: R5's central claim is that it "verified on disk" that only three columns hold rendered storage URLs, and that this "converts this from an open-ended migration into a two-release change with a countable gate." The enumeration is incomplete. profiles.avatar_url stores a full couple_media public URL: E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart:52-59 uploads to `couple_media` and calls getPublicUrl, and E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/supabase_repository.dart:351-355 writes that string into profiles.avatar_url. It appears in neither R5's MIGRATED list nor R2's P-REL column table, so D7 step (a) never normalises it, the unmatched-prefix counter never counts it, and every user's avatar becomes a broken image at step (d) — the exact silent failure R5 says the enumeration exists to prevent. R5's invariant_after compounds it by enforcing the rule against "the checked-in media-column list," the enumeration form that GRANT-LANDMINE argues, correctly, always rots.
findings.repair: Add profiles.avatar_url to D7 step (a) and to the D7 column list. Replace the checked-in media-column list with a catalogue-driven assertion that cannot go stale: for every text/varchar/jsonb column of every table in `public`, assert no value matches '/storage/v1/object/public/' — run against seed data in CI and as a sampled conformance check (same 1,000-newest-rows bound R3 uses for bucket_path_shape) in production. That form would have found avatar_url without anyone remembering it.

findings.problem: Shared contract §5 deletes presence's `couple:<id>:msg` and puts typing on `ch:<couple_id>:<recipient_uid>`, whose gate is couple membership, claiming "Presence's requirement is satisfied exactly, with one fewer channel per device." It is inverted. presence.md puts typing on `:live` and chat on `:msg` precisely because realtime.messages RLS cannot see a broadcast's event name (presence.md:73, :309: "a single channel forces the privacy toggle to either leak typing or break chat delivery"). Its invariant ("One reciprocal boolean gates presence.read/write and broadcast.read/write on couple:<id>:live in both directions"), its accepted limit 6, its open decision 3 and its verification item (e) — "assert the peer receives zero presence frames and zero broadcast frames on couple:<id>:live" — all depend on share_presence=false suppressing typing. Under §5, share_presence=false leaves typing flowing on ch:. §5 chose "leak typing" without saying so, in an app whose premise is concealment. Related and also unresolved: transport §A puts the receipt-watermark hint on `cl:`, messaging puts it on the chat topic; §5 does not say, and on cl: the privacy toggle would silently kill read receipts.
findings.repair: Typing stays on `cl:`, which §5's own table already gates on reciprocal share_presence. `ch:` becomes server-write-only, carrying the chat doorbell and the receipt-watermark hint only — which is strictly better, because it removes the last client-writable private topic outside cl:/rt: and makes §5 consistent with the cs:/dev: doctrine. State in §5 that the receipt hint rides ch: and is therefore outside the privacy predicate, and keep presence.md's UI copy unchanged.

findings.problem: R2 gates the drop of public.presence (Stage M) on "a CI grep proving zero `.from('presence')` call sites remain in mobile/lib." That is a repository gate, not a fleet gate, and this app is sideloaded with no update channel. Verified 7 live call sites in the shipped build: presence_service.dart:191, :372, :385; session_provider.dart:156, :181, :187; supabase_repository.dart:331. presence.md's own cutover doctrine already rejects this shape — "because flipping privacy on an existing topic name is a breaking change between app versions and this app is sideloaded, the cutover is version-gated, not time-gated" — and R2 replaces that with a grep for the one step in the plan that is irreversible. An installed build upserting into a dropped table gets a hard PostgREST error on every presence write.
findings.repair: Stage M's gate is the repo grep AND observed adoption of min_client_build through app_runtime_config, the mechanism presence.md already specifies for its own topic cutover — plus a release-gap in which the table exists, is written by nobody, and is confirmed to have zero writes via pg_stat_user_tables before the drop. Same two-release shape R5 correctly applies to D7.

findings.problem: Neither the eight resolutions nor the shared contract reconciles calling.md's own position space with the couple stream, and R1 explicitly preserves both halves of the conflict ("§I is unaffected — call signalling still uses stream='call' on couple_stream"). calling.md's invariant allocates `calls.signal_seq` under the `calls` row lock and its catch-up is `seq > cursor order by seq` on call_signals; transport §I puts those same rows on couple_stream with a `pos` from next_pos. So call_signals would carry two positions, two orderings and two catch-up paths, violating contract §1's own rule that "every streamed table has exactly one [position column], named by its stream_registry row," and leaving unstated which one the client's cursor uses. Secondary, also unstated: calling's end_call NULLs every call_signals.payload for the call in one UPDATE. call_signals is in the stream vocabulary, transport's allocator is a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE row trigger, and §1's mutation rule requires exactly one position per payload alteration — so end_call silently costs one position and one cs: doorbell per signal row.
findings.repair: Decide one. Recommend: call_signals is a streamed table carrying stream_pos from next_pos and no signal_seq — the couple_cursor lock gives a strictly stronger ordering than the per-call lock it replaces, and calling.md's ring path already does not depend on the stream. Register it in stream_registry accordingly and delete calls.signal_seq from calling.md §1 and its catch-up query. Then grant end_call the same bulk-suppression idiom §1 already grants the purge: set_config('miles.bulk_purge','1',true), one op='update' position for the whole nulling statement. Note this interacts with F4: end_call must not hold the allocator lock across a wide UPDATE.

findings.problem: GRANT-LANDMINE deletes retention enable-gate condition (ii) and explicitly re-affirms (i) trigger-stamped and (iii) leading-column index. Three of data.md's own initial registry entries cannot satisfy the surviving conditions, so the sweeper fails closed and writes a page-severity ops_event on every run from D6 onward. (a) cron.job_run_details and (b) net._http_response are extension-owned tables outside `public`: their timestamps cannot be BEFORE-trigger-stamped, so (i) fails permanently — and data.md §8 names exactly these two as the entries that "grow forever on a 500 MB database." (c) The only call_invites index data.md §6 specifies is (couple_id, created_at desc), whose leading column is couple_id, so (iii) fails for the 10-minute SDP-null entry that exists to stop a stale invite staying answerable. No resolution addresses this, and the reconciliation's repeated argument is that a permanently-red page alarm on a single-maintainer project is the failure mode that kills the whole observability design.
findings.repair: Scope the gate to tables the project owns in `public`. Add mode='extension_ttl' for extension-owned tables: a stated bound, an ops_expectation on the effective setting where one exists (pg_net.ttl), no trigger requirement, and an SLI on row count rather than a sweeper. Add the index `call_invites(created_at)` in the same migration that inserts its registry row, and retire the entry to mode='partition_drop' when calling S3 lands. Add a CI assertion that every enabled retention_policy row passes its own gate at insert time, so an unsatisfiable entry cannot be committed at all.

findings.problem: The shared contract leaves the push↔client background contradiction unresolved, and in doing so leaves data.md's only delivery-health SLI unimplementable. client.md is categorical: "the FCM background isolate may write a sync_due marker and post a notification; it may not drain and it may not apply" (§E, §M). push.md §7 requires a background catch-up that advances push_devices.cursor_seq and a push_receipts ack within ~3 s, and its headline ≈12 pushes/user/day figure is a direct output of cursor_seq suppression. data.md's FATAL 3 closure names accepted_not_delivered (outbox rows with fcm_accepted_at older than N minutes and no matching push_receipts row) as THE delivery metric, replacing state='dead'. Contract §2(c) blesses cursor_seq as "an OPTIMISATION INPUT, never an invariant" but never says which isolate writes it or writes a receipt. If the client rule holds as written, push_receipts is never written from a background wake, so accepted_not_delivered is permanently saturated and the one alarm data.md defines is useless.
findings.repair: Name the exception explicitly in the contract: the background isolate may issue exactly two writes — a push_receipts ack and a greatest()-guarded push_devices.cursor_seq advance — both zero-parameter RPCs, neither touching the entity mirror, the outbox or any cursor the sync engine owns, so client.md's convergence argument is untouched. Add it to client.md §E and §M as a named allowlist entry and to push.md as a client prerequisite. If that write is judged unaffordable inside the background budget, say so and replace accepted_not_delivered with an SLI that does not depend on it.

findings.problem: GRANT-LANDMINE's headline assertion is `select count(*) ... where n.nspname='public' and a.attacl is not null` must be ZERO, wired to a page-severity conformance expectation every 60 s. Two gaps. First, after D1a revokes the frozen column grants, Postgres may leave attacl as an empty aclitem array rather than resetting it to NULL; the resolution asserts "attacl is populated ONLY when a column-level grant or revoke has actually been issued" without verifying the post-revoke state, and if it is wrong the page alarm is red from the day D1a lands. Second, D1a never states HOW the ACL is removed. An enumerated column-level REVOKE is itself a column-level revoke and violates the rule the same migration installs; a table-level `REVOKE UPDATE ON profiles FROM authenticated` also clears the corresponding column privileges and needs no enumeration, but the resolution does not say this and CI assertion 1 needs a named carve-out either way. On the stress question itself: assertion 3 WOULD have caught gender/gender_set — it is byte-for-byte the /role-setup dead end documented at newuser_fixes.sql:158-172, it fails against today's frozen list, and assertion 2's single-scalar form does cover INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT without enumerating anything.
findings.repair: State the violation predicate as `attacl is not null and cardinality(attacl) > 0`, which is correct under both Postgres behaviours and costs nothing. State D1a's exact form as table-level statements (revoke update on public.profiles from authenticated, anon; grant update on public.profiles to authenticated; same shape for capsules; revoke all on public.vault_pin from authenticated, anon) and name that one migration as the single exemption to CI assertion 1, in the manifest.

findings.problem: R4's admission test forbids its own dispatcher. The rule is "a job qualifies for a cron slot ONLY if its required cadence is below 60 seconds" enforced by "a CI grep failing any migration that calls cron.schedule with an interval >= 60 s," and manifest slot 2 is ops_tick at exactly 60 s. Separately, R4 places calling's reaper as an ops_job at schedule_seconds 60 dispatched by a 60 s tick that "takes a non-blocking advisory lock (a still-running tick is skipped, never queued)" — so its effective cadence is 60–120 s, not 60 s, and R4's claim that "30 s to 60 s costs nothing" is really 30 s to 60–120 s.
findings.repair: State the CI rule as "> 60 s", with ops_tick named in cron_job_manifest as the single 60 s exemption because it is the dispatcher. Restate the reaper's cadence as 60–120 s effective and cite calling.md's own statement that nothing correctness-bearing depends on it, so the widening is recorded rather than discovered.

findings.problem: Shared contract §9 is the anti-recurrence mechanism, and its trigger list does not cover the classes that produced most of the conflicts it is reconciling. A migration must register a bucket, cron job, partitioned table, retention entry, stream, realtime topic class or allocator. It need NOT register: a new outbox or device table (the three-outbox conflict, contract §6); a new per-entity counter or position space (calling's calls.signal_seq, F9 — it is not a per-couple allocator, so R1's CI assertion passes); a client data-class assignment (STREAM/SNAPSHOT/SESSION, client.md §A); a topic payload assignment and the privacy predicate that governs it (F7); or a column that stores a rendered storage URL (F6). So §9 covers the six ROADMAP conflicts and not the class of the conflicts.
findings.repair: Extend §9's trigger list and the registry set to {outbox/device table, counter or position space of any scope, topic payload assignment with its governing privacy predicate, storage-URL-bearing column, client data-class assignment}, each with an owner row in table_owner and a set-equality conformance check where the fact is observable in the catalogue. The test of §9 is whether re-running the original consistency audit against the contract finds nothing; as written it would still find F7 and F9.

findings.problem: The audit's open finding that ops_expectation "is the comparand for the entire conformance mechanism and is verified against nothing" is answered for exactly one class — contract §4 makes the realtime topic predicate a SECURITY DEFINER function body, notes correctly that "a function body is DDL, so supabase db diff and the migration checksum both cover it," and says this "closes the audit's ops_expectation-is-unverified-reference-data finding for this class." Contract §9 then creates five more row-shaped comparands (stream_registry, cron_job_manifest, realtime_topic_registry, bucket_map, table_owner) and makes set equality against them the enforcement for buckets, cron slots, streams, topics and ownership. Every one of those is a row that db diff cannot see, edited by the same hand that would edit the object it guards. The net effect of the reconciliation on this finding is negative.
findings.repair: Express each registry as the return of an immutable SQL function checked into migrations, so db diff and schema_migration_checksum both cover it, and keep the table only as a materialisation that conformance compares against the function. That is the same repair §4 already applies to the RLS helper, generalised — it costs five function bodies and removes the last unverified comparand.

findings.problem: data.md requires every RLS exemption to carry an expires_at and makes an expired exemption itself a violation. The audit flagged that this manufactures a recurring violation stream on the ~10 internal tables that must permanently have zero policies (couple_cursor, couple_stream, couple_member_cursor, push_outbox, push_receipts, retention_policy, ops_* , schema_migration_checksum). No resolution addresses it, and the reconciliation enlarges the population: user_status (R2), and the five registries plus table_owner (§9), all internal, all permanently policy-free.
findings.repair: Split the concept into two committed sets: no_policy_by_design (permanent, no expires_at, and additionally asserted to hold zero grants to authenticated or anon — which is a stronger check than a policy would be) and ops_rule_exemption (temporary, expires_at mandatory, expiry is a violation). Place couple_cursor, the four registries, table_owner and user_status in the first, and state that R3's pre-D7 public-bucket exemption is the model case for the second.

invariants_broken:
Five named invariants of four designs are broken by the resolutions as written, plus one that is silently inverted.

1) messaging.md, "ISSUED-RANGE CONTIGUITY, NOT ROW CONTIGUITY (SERVER-ENFORCED + BY CONSTRUCTION)" — broken by R1's invariant_after (d), which defines the canary as contiguity of messages.cseq per couple. Rows leave messages routinely (verified: clear_chat_everyone.sql / chat_media_cleanup.sql hard-delete every row for the couple), and two clears leave a permanent hole because clear rows survive subsequent clears. REPAIR in F2: canary asserts chat_seq >= max(cseq), uniqueness, contiguity only above max(clear_through_cseq), and that every surviving row at or below that floor is kind='clear'.

2) messaging.md, "EXACTLY ONE CSEQ PER STREAM-MUTATING OPERATION (SERVER-ENFORCED, LOAD-BEARING)" together with send_message's stated step order ("the lock comes first, before anything else ... return the original without bumping the counter") — broken by R1's single-UPDATE allocation, which increments before the dedup branch and burns a cseq on every retried send the server already committed. REPAIR in F3: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then dedup, then the increment. Non-chat streams keep the single UPDATE.

3) presence.md, "PRIVACY IS A PREDICATE EVALUATED INSIDE THE REALTIME SERVER" plus accepted limit 6 and verification item (e) — broken by shared contract §5, which moves typing onto the membership-gated ch: topic so share_presence=false no longer suppresses it. REPAIR in F7: typing stays on cl:; ch: becomes server-write-only and carries the chat doorbell and the receipt hint.

4) transport.md, "POSITION ORDER IS COMMIT ORDER, AND ALLOCATION IS UNBYPASSABLE" is preserved, but transport §C's cost model for it is not: R1 merges two lock domains onto one tuple and asserts "nothing is paid for it," which converts transport's locally-accepted "purge briefly blocks the partner's sends" into cross-domain head-of-line blocking of calling's signal path inside a 45 s ring. REPAIR in F4: two allocator rows in one allocator table, or a rule forbidding the allocator lock to be held across a bulk DELETE.

5) shared contract §1, "Every streamed table has exactly one position column, named by its stream_registry row" — broken by the contract's own preservation of calling.md's calls.signal_seq alongside transport §I's stream='call' on couple_stream, so call_signals carries two positions and two catch-up paths. REPAIR in F9: call_signals keeps stream_pos only; calls.signal_seq is withdrawn.

6) Inverted rather than broken — client.md's "NO SCREEN MAY ISSUE A NETWORK REQUEST" and "the background isolate may not drain and may not apply" versus push.md §7's background receipt ack and cursor_seq advance. Contract §2(c) blesses cursor_seq without saying who writes it, leaving data.md's accepted_not_delivered SLI — its entire FATAL 3 closure — unimplementable. REPAIR in F11: name the two permitted background writes as an explicit allowlist entry.

Two resolutions break nothing and should be adopted as written: R3 (all buckets private permanently; crypto never argued public was better and its verification 7(c) rewrite is correct) and R6 (partitioning is a stage not a threshold; the runway-alarm scoping to strategy='range' is a real latent defect caught, and hash tables must be exempt by kind rather than by an expiring exemption row).
verdict:
Not shippable as written. The reconciliation is substantially better than what it replaces — R3 and R6 are clean and should be adopted verbatim, R4's manifest-plus-admission-test is the right shape, R5's single-owner call is correct, and GRANT-LANDMINE's move from "guard the mechanism" to "delete the mechanism" is the strongest decision in the set — but sixteen findings survive, one of them fatal, and three of the four resolutions I was asked to stress hardest each move part of their conflict rather than closing it.

R1, stressed on concurrency: the dense-counter fix DOES hold where the question aims. Two counters on one tuple contend on the same row lock, so a chat insert and a reach insert to the same couple serialize, the loser blocks to COMMIT, and both counters are commit-ordered and dense — a rolled-back transaction releases its value rather than burning it, unlike nextval. Neither concurrent inserts to different streams nor the data domain's single-allocator ordering guarantee is the problem. Three other things are. The allocation is specified as one UPDATE, which increments before send_message's dedup check and therefore burns a cseq on every retry — the exact property messaging.md's step order exists to protect (F3). The canary is specified as row contiguity, which is the assertion messaging.md deleted as the cause of its own FATAL 2, and it goes permanently red on the second clear (F2). And the merge silently couples two lock domains that were independent, so a chat clear now blocks call signalling inside the ring window, against a claim that "nothing is paid for it" (F4). The backfill rule is separately wrong: every streamed table is `id uuid default gen_random_uuid()`, so ordering by id is ordering at random and shuffles all historical stream order to avoid misordering the few rows a client could have forged (F5).

CLIENT-F2, stressed on both halves: the mechanism is right and the two questions asked both resolve in its favour. The tombstone does not need to survive a hard DELETE, because the only hard-delete path is clear_conversation_everyone (verified as a bare couple-wide DELETE in clear_chat_everyone.sql, with chat_media_cleanup.sql adding the storage half), and the clear is itself a control row at a higher cseq carrying clear_through_cseq, which supersedes any redact or hide it destroys. A client offline for the entire episode genuinely learns, by either path independently: below its cursor it is served the already-stripped target, above it the control row, and — the case that actually decides it — a reinstalled client parked above install_floor still learns, because fetch_history returns the target with body/media nulled and deleted_by appended, so the redundancy argument survives the one path that mints no token. Display order is genuinely preserved. What is wrong is not the mechanism but where it is put: the resolution lands the messages INSERT revoke in messaging Stage 1, and the entire installed fleet sends by direct PostgREST insert at chat_repository.dart:228/249/279/309 while messaging Stage 1 explicitly requires those inserts to keep working. On a sideloaded app with no update channel that is a fleet-wide send outage with no rollback (F1).

GRANT-LANDMINE, stressed on the assertion: yes, assertion 3 would have caught gender/gender_set. It is byte-for-byte the /role-setup dead end documented in newuser_fixes.sql:158-172, it fails against today's frozen column list, and it is the right regression test. Assertion 2 is the better idea of the two — a single scalar over pg_attribute.attacl covers INSERT, UPDATE, SELECT and every future verb and table without enumerating anything, which is exactly the property data.md's per-verb has_column_privilege loop lacked. Two loose ends only: the violation predicate should be `attacl is not null and cardinality(attacl) > 0` rather than `attacl is not null`, because a post-revoke empty aclitem array would otherwise make a page-severity alarm red from the day D1a lands; and D1a never states how the ACL is removed, which matters because an enumerated column-level REVOKE violates the rule the same migration installs (F12).

On completeness: the shared contract covers the six conflicts the ROADMAP named plus the two the audit escalated, and §9 is a genuine anti-recurrence mechanism — but it covers the six that happened to be found, not their class. The supplied audit only ever examined two of eight domains (data and client; CROSS-DOMAIN-GAPS.json has exactly two entries), so the domain pairs it never reviewed still contain live conflicts, and the largest one is in the pair the contract touches most: calling.md's calls.signal_seq versus transport §I's stream='call' on couple_stream, two positions over the same rows, which §9 cannot catch because a per-call counter is not a per-couple allocator (F9). The same blind spot produced F7 (no registry for which channel a payload rides or which privacy predicate governs it) and F6 (no registry for a column holding a rendered storage URL — and profiles.avatar_url, missed by R5's "verified" enumeration, is that hole already open). Four audit findings the reconciliation does not answer at all remain: the unsatisfiable retention gate on three of data.md's own entries (F10), the push/client background-write contradiction that leaves data.md's only delivery SLI dead (F11), the unverified-comparand problem which §9 makes five times larger (F15), and mandatory expires_at on permanently policy-free internal tables (F16). Fix F1 before anything ships; F2, F3, F4 and F5 are all edits to R1's own text and cost nothing; F6 through F11 are decisions that must be taken rather than inherited.
